CIA-UAP-D027, Office of Scientific Intelligence Briefing on “Flying Saucers,” 1952
CIA-UAP-D027、科学情報局による「空飛ぶ円盤」に関する報告、1952 年
CIA
CIA
11/20/26
2026年11月20日（Release 08）
8/14/52
Washington, D.C.
ワシントン D.C.
PDF
PDF
This 14 August 1952 Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Office of Scientific Intelligence (OSI) briefing evaluates the U.S. Air Force’s investigation of “flying saucer” reports and considers their potential intelligence implications. OSI prepared the briefing amid heightened public and official interest following an increase in reports during July 1952 and recent public statements by U.S. Air Force officials. The briefing summarizes the history of reported sightings, the Air Technical Intelligence Center’s (ATIC) reporting and analytical processes, selected unexplained cases, and several theories advanced to explain the reports. The materials state that approximately 1,500 official reports had been received since 1947, including 250 during July 1952, and that ATIC categorized approximately 20 percent as unexplained. It states that OSI reviewed its own intelligence holdings, official reports, press and popular accounts, and Soviet press indexes; consulted an Air Force special-study representative and ATIC personnel at Wright Field; and sought input from selected scientific consultants. The briefing states that OSI recommended no further action following those inquiries.
この 1952 年 8 月 14 日の中央情報局 (CIA) 科学情報局 (OSI) のブリーフィングでは、アメリカ空軍による「空飛ぶ円盤」報告書の調査を評価し、その潜在的なインテリジェンスへの影響を検討しています。 OSIは、1952年7月中の報告の増加と米空軍関係者による最近の公式声明を受けて、国民および政府の関心が高まっている中でこの説明会を準備した。このブリーフィングでは、報告された目撃情報の歴史、航空技術情報センター（ATIC）の報告と分析のプロセス、選択された未解明の事例、および報告を説明するために進められたいくつかの理論が要約されています。資料には、1947年以来約1,500件の公式報告書が受領され、その中には1952年7月中の250件が含まれており、ATICは約20％を原因不明として分類したと述べている。それは、OSIが自らの諜報所蔵資料、公式報告書、報道機関や一般の報道、ソ連の報道指標を調査したと述べている。ライトフィールドの空軍特別研究代表者とATIC職員に​​相談した。そして選ばれた科学コンサルタントから意見を求めました。会見では、OSIはこれらの問い合わせを受けてそれ以上の行動をとらないよう勧告したと述べている。

1952年8月の機関向けブリーフィング要旨。空軍のフライング・ソーサー報告急増を受け、機関は空軍研究（ATIC/Project Saucer）と公刊情報、ソ連報道、専門家らの意見をレビューした。1947年のKenneth Arnold目撃以降、1948年のProject Saucer、1949年の予備報告と一部公表、1951年の再開と世界的報告体制の導入などが経緯として示される。代表的事例としてMantell機墜落（1948年）、Gormanの夜間追尾（1948年）、White Sandsでの高機動目撃（1949年）や、Sandy Hook・Fort Monmouthや極東空母、Wright Fieldでの視覚・レーダーの一致例（F-94の写真ネガティブ含む）が挙げられている。報告は約1,500件（当月だけで250件）にのぼり、ATICは全体の約20%を未解明と分類した。目撃の特徴は昼間の金属光沢を持つ球・楕円体や多様な形状、夜間の各種光、速度はホバリング〜通常航空機〜極高速（White Sandsで18,000mphとされる例）、最大約20gの加速、音や痕跡の欠如、接近時の回避行動などである。公表されている主要理論は（1）米国極秘兵器（政府高官が否定）、（2）ソ連開発（支持情報なし）、（3）地球外起源（証拠無し）、（4）空軍の立場である既知物の誤認または未解明の自然現象であり、結論として行動提言は示されていない。ブリーフィングは機関関心の外部流出が公衆不安を増幅する危険があると注意している。
Briefing summary (14 Aug 1952) reviewing Air Force and Agency examination of the surge in flying saucer reports. The Agency reviewed internal intelligence back to 1946, official reports, press and books, Soviet press indexes, interviewed Air Force Special Study Group, met ATIC officers at Wright Field, and consulted outside scientific advisers. Historical milestones noted: 1947 Kenneth Arnold sighting, Project Saucer (1948), ATIC preliminary report (Apr 1949), partial secret report release (Dec 1949), and study reopening with worldwide reporting in 1951. Notable incidents include Captain Mantell's fatal pursuit (1948), Lt. Gorman's dogfight at Fargo (1948), multiple White Sands sightings (1949), and combined visual/radar cases (Sandy Hook/Fort Monmouth, a Far East carrier report, and an F-94 intercept at Wright Field with a camera negative). About 1,500 official reports exist (250 in the cited July); ATIC classifies ~20% as unexplained. Reported characteristics: daytime metallic spherical/elliptical and varied shapes, nighttime lights, speeds from hovering to moderate to extremely high (an 18,000 mph claim at White Sands), occasional violent maneuvering (<10%), accelerations up to ~20g, general absence of sound or vapor trails, and evasive behavior on approach. Radar showed many unidentified blips but no continuous station-to-station tracks. Four major public theories are summarized: U.S. secret weapon (officially denied), Soviet development (no supporting intelligence), extraterrestrial visitors (no evidence), and the Air Force view—that sightings can be misidentifications of known objects or poorly understood natural phenomena. No action recommendations were made; the briefing cautions against publicizing Agency interest to avoid aggravating public concern.

CIA-UAP-D029, Official Diary Entry on “Flying Saucers,” 1952
CIA-UAP-D029、「空飛ぶ円盤」に関する公式日記エントリ、1952 年

This 28 October 1952 entry in a Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) official diary records a discussion of new information concerning “flying saucers.” Mr. Clark reported that CIA had received additional information, including reports of objects observed from the ground by individuals the entry characterized as relatively reliable. The entry notes that the absence of reported noise or flaring associated with certain reports posed a theoretical difficulty for interpreting them. It further states that several scientists had presented papers describing a possible propulsion method that would not involve noise or flares. Dr. Clark proposed a briefing on the subject and recommended bringing the information to the attention of the U.S. Air Force and the Research and Development Board; the diary’s author concurred.
中央情報局 (CIA) の公式日記の 1952 年 10 月 28 日の記述には、「空飛ぶ円盤」に関する新情報についての議論が記録されています。クラーク氏は、CIAが追加情報を受け取ったと報告した。その中には、比較的信頼できると特徴付けられた入国者によって地上から観察された物体の報告も含まれていた。このエントリでは、特定のレポートに関連するノイズやフレアが報告されていないため、それらを解釈するのが理論​​的に困難になっていると述べています。さらに、数人の科学者が騒音やフレアを伴わない推進方法の可能性を説明する論文を発表したと述べている。クラーク博士は、この件に関する説明会を提案し、その情報を米空軍と研究開発委員会に知らせるよう勧告した。日記の筆者も同意した。

DOW-UAP-D165, Unresolved Radar Detection, North America, 2023
DOW-UAP-D165、未解決のレーダー探知、北米、2023
Department of War
米国戦争省
11/20/26
2026年11月20日（Release 08）
7/15/05
Western United States
米国西部
PDF
PDF
This slide summarizes the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office’s (AARO) preliminary analysis of an unresolved radar event in the western United States. In 2023, a civil air-surveillance radar system recorded eight detections over 84 seconds at an estimated altitude of 55,000–70,000 feet. If the detections were associated with a single continuous track, their cumulative point-to-point displacement would be approximately 38.5 miles, yielding a minimum mean horizontal ground-speed estimate of 1,650 mph. Successive detection segments also showed an apparent 39-degree change in bearing after approximately 48 seconds, although the available data are not sufficient to enable a comprehensive kinematic characterization. Available data do not independently establish that all detections originated from the same object or represented a continuous track. The nature and origin of the detections remain unresolved due to data insufficiency.
このスライドは、米国西部で発生した未解決のレーダー イベントに関する全ドメイン異常解決局 (AARO) の予備分析を要約したものです。 2023 年、民間航空監視レーダー システムは、推定高度 55,000 ～ 70,000 フィートで 84 秒間に 8 件の探知を記録しました。検出が単一の連続軌道に関連付けられている場合、それらの累積点間変位は約 38.5 マイルとなり、最小平均水平対地速度推定値は 1,650 マイルになります。連続した検出セグメントでも、約 48 秒後に方位に明らかな 39 度の変化が示されましたが、入手可能なデータは包括的​​な運動学的特性評価を可能にするのに十分ではありません。入手可能なデータは、すべての検出が同じ物体から発生したものであること、または連続した軌跡を表していることを独立して確立するものではありません。データ不足のため、検出の性質と起源は未解決のままです。

Successive point‑to‑point segments show an apparent ~39° counter‑clockwise change in bearing after ~48 seconds. The radar sweep interval is 12 seconds, which is insufficient to independently establish that all eight detections originated from the same object or represent a continuous track. Figure notes: green/red points = commercial air traffic; red line connects detections in sequence using shortest straight‑line distances; blue areas = weather data; highlighted area = reported detections over time, not a reconstructed trajectory. The report describes apparent supersonic kinematics.

This document is an administrative, programmatic, or contractor-produced record related to the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP), a Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)-administered program active from 2008 to 2012. AAWSAP’s official scope of work identified 12 technical research areas relating to potential aerospace threats over a time horizon of more than 40 years. As part of the broader program record, the file documents how AAWSAP was scoped, organized, tasked, funded, executed, or described at a particular point in time. This file contains a program report produced by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS), summarizing its work under the AAWSAP contract through July 30, 2009, while also including substantial forward-looking discussion of planned or proposed work. It includes unresolved internal process questions and comparative assessments of equipment options. In addition to documenting the production of a series of technical research papers, the report describes archival and documentary research concerning historical incidents reported to involve unidentified anomalous phenomena. The report also documents BAASS inquiries into parapsychological and paranormal phenomena, including research activities at a Utah site with a reported history of anomalous activity.

This document is an Air Intelligence Information Report (AIIR), a standardized U.S. Air Force reporting form used to record raw information of potential intelligence value for later analysis. The form served as a primary vehicle for U.S. Air Force field intelligence collection throughout the early Cold War, until defense-wide reporting standards were established in the early 1960s. This AIIR records an October 12, 1957, incident 800 yards off Martha’s Vineyard and one to two miles east-southeast of Woods Hole, Massachusetts. At approximately 2035Z (4:35 p.m. local time), a group of two Air Force officers, two sailing masters assigned to research vessels with the Oceangraph Institute, and a civilian reported observing a cylindrical, metallic-colored object with protrusions while fishing. The report describes the object as appearing to descend rapidly, changing direction twice, and disappearing at high speed after approximately 20 seconds. The reporting office stated that it did not conduct further investigation or analysis of the report. All descriptive and estimative language contained in this report reflects the reporter’s subjective interpretation at the time of the event. Such characterizations should not be interpreted as a conclusive indication of the presence or absence of any intrinsic object features or performance characteristics.

Onufer, Capt. Scott Bray, Capt. Gene Maysona, and Mr. Ronald Veeder) reported an unidentified object about 1–2 miles ESE of Woodshole (also described as ~800 yards off Martha’s Vineyard). Object described as cylindrical, nickel/aluminum appearance, with trihedral protrusions on front, rear and sides; no windows or markings reported. Observation was ground visual with binoculars, duration about 20 seconds. Initial appearance was a rapid descent, then it slowed, moved right, reversed to left, reversed again to the right and disappeared at high speed; it became wavy/blurred before fading and was reported to disappear toward the sun. Weather clear, visibility ~15 miles. Approximately 30 minutes after the sighting a C-121 was observed conducting apparent touch-and-go operations at Otis AFB. The source (G. R. Onufer) is assessed as reliable (USAF flight experience). The observers telephoned Otis AFB operations but returned to Charleston before confirming completion of the report. No further investigation was conducted due to distance and likelihood that action had already been taken.

This AIIR documents an October 13, 1957, incident involving an unidentified flying object (UFO) near Indian Trails on Lake Erie, Michigan. At approximately 10:05 p.m. local time, two observers reported a single silver-gray, bell-shaped object, with an apparent size comparable to a basketball, and a visible division between its upper and lower sections, featuring possible lights or portholes, and emitting a high-pitched humming sound. The report estimated the object’s speed at about 225 mph and distance from the observers to be approximately 150 yards. Such characterizations should not be interpreted as a conclusive indication of the presence or absence of any intrinsic object features or performance characteristics.

This memorandum requests approval in principle for a Central Intelligence Agency-sponsored external research project focusing on Unidentified Flying Objects (UFOs). The proposed effort would convene an ad hoc panel of leading scientists to analyze and evaluate available UFO evidence and recommend any further government action warranted to address the matter. The memorandum describes the project as an important component of the office’s effort to improve intelligence on UFOs and support an Office of Scientific Intelligence task force working with the U.S. Air Force since 20 August 1952. Although the memorandum is undated, its reference to Dr. Max Millikan as Director of CENIS (a position he held 1951-1952) and to the ongoing Air Force collaboration supports a late-1952 date.

This circa 2 October 1952 draft memorandum from Central Intelligence Agency Director Walter B. Smith to the Director of the Psychological Strategy Board transmits a proposal to the National Security Council concerning “Flying Saucers,” or Unidentified Flying Objects (UFOs). The memorandum states that UFO-related issues may have implications for psychological warfare, intelligence, and operations, and recommends that the Board discuss potential offensive and defensive psychological warfare considerations. Documents in the file summarize the issue, describe related Air Force investigative activity, and identify intelligence and research questions concerning the reported phenomena, including possible implications for U.S. national security. The materials state that, since 1947, the U.S. Government had received approximately 1,500 official reports of UFO sightings, in addition to a substantial volume of letters, telephone calls, and press reports from the public. They further state that the Air Force considered approximately 20 percent of the official reports unexplained, with a higher unexplained rate reported for cases received during 1952. The attached proposal recommended a centrally administered research program under the Research and Development Board to address operational, intelligence, and psychological-warfare requirements identified by the Secretary of Defense, the Director of Central Intelligence, and the Director of the Psychological Strategy Board.
1952年10月2日頃、ウォルター・B・スミス中央情報局長官から心理戦略委員会長官に宛てられたこの覚書草案は、「空飛ぶ円盤」すなわち未確認飛行物体（UFO）に関する提案を国家安全保障会議に送付するも​​のである。覚書では、UFO関連の問題は心理戦、諜報活動、作戦に影響を与える可能性があると述べ、理事会が潜在的な攻撃的および防御的な心理戦の考慮事項について議論することを勧告している。ファイル内の文書は問題を要約し、関連する空軍の調査活動を説明し、米国の国家安全保障への影響の可能性を含む、報告された現象に関する情報と研究上の疑問を特定します。資料には、1947年以来、米国政府が一般からの相当量の手紙、電話、報道に加えて、約1,500件のUFO目撃に関する公式報告を受け取ったと記載されている。さらに、空軍は公式報告の約20パーセントが原因不明であり、1952年中に報告された事件では原因不明の割合がより高いとみなしていると述べている。添付の提案書は、国防長官、中央情報局長官、心理戦略委員会長官が特定した作戦、諜報、心理戦の要件に対処するため、研究開発委員会の下で集中管理される研究プログラムを推奨している。

中央情報局長名の覚書で、未確認飛行物体（飛行円盤）に関する問題が情報・作戦だけでなく心理戦にも含意を持つとして国家安全保障会議あての提案（TAB A）を送付したことを伝えている。TABでは、1947年以降約1600件の目撃報告や多数の一般通報・報道があり、ライト・フィールドの空軍技術情報センター(ATIC)の小規模な管理班（将校2名・秘書2名）が報告収集・分類を行っている事実を示す。現行手法は各事例を「説明できる/説明できない」に分類する歴史的処理であり、MITの顧問らは多くの事例が現有の大気学・気象学知識の最前線かその周辺にあり、核廃棄物の副産物等が要因の可能性もあると指摘した。結論として識別能力など作戦上の問題を第一義としつつ、（1）これら現象が制御可能で軍事的・心理的利用に供するか、（2）予測可能か否か、（3）ソ連の知識・意図・能力の有無といった点を明らかにするための中枢的研究・情報責任の指定が必要とされる。勧告は短期・長期の行動を分け、短期的には研究開発局（RDB）配下での政府主導の研究プログラム設置（1947年安全保障法21条(a)に基づく）とPsychological Strategy Boardへの報告、国防長官による調整と情報担当者の指名を促すものであった。さらに質問票、重要要素の抽出、時系列・地域比較、データ属性の客観的研究などの標準的解析手法を用いることが提案され、現時点で空軍からの支援と分析の範囲が限定的であるため解釈には限界があると結んでいる。
A CIA memorandum to the Director of the Psychological Strategy Board reports transmitting a proposal to the National Security Council concluding that unidentified flying objects have implications for psychological warfare as well as intelligence and operations. The TAB summarizes factual findings: since 1947 about 1,600 sightings and numerous letters/press reports have been received; collection and initial analysis are handled by a small Air Technical Intelligence Center (ATIC) unit at Wright Field (two officers, two secretaries). Current practice classifies incidents as explained or unexplained, a method judged limited; MIT consultants advised that many phenomena may lie at or beyond current atmospheric knowledge and noted possible factors such as nuclear waste byproducts. The memorandum treats identification and operational problems as primary and recommends clarifying whether the phenomena are controllable/useable for military or psychological purposes, whether they are predictable, and what the Soviet knowledge, intent, or capability might be. Recommendations call for short- and long-term actions, including establishing a centrally administered research program under the Research and Development Board (RDB) per the 1947 National Security Act (Sec. 21(a)), assigning intelligence responsibilities, and Secretary of Defense coordination. Standard analytical methods (surveys, isolating key elements, trend/area studies, objective study of data attributes) are proposed. It notes that limited central support and narrow prior analysis constrain current interpretations.

This 1 August 1952 memorandum from Edward Tauss, Acting Chief of the Weapons and Equipment Division in the Central Intelligence Agency’s (CIA) Office of Scientific Intelligence, provides an initial assessment of “flying saucers” and associated reports. The memorandum states that the Air Technical Intelligence Center had received between 1,000 and 2,000 reports, many of which it assessed as false, attributable to known U.S. equipment, or explainable as natural phenomena. It states that fewer than 100 reasonably credible reports remained unexplained and that the available information did not identify a consistent pattern in their reported characteristics or locations. The memorandum recommends that CIA continue to monitor the issue in coordination with the Air Technical Intelligence Center while avoiding public disclosure of CIA interest. It also notes that Tauss had arranged a comprehensive briefing with the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base for 8 August 1952 and would prepare a detailed analysis afterward.

CIA-UAP-D028, Assessment of National Security Issues Relating to “Flying Saucers,” 1952
CIA-UAP-D028、「空飛ぶ円盤」に関する国家安全保障問題の評価、1952 年

This 13 October 1952 memorandum from S. Q. Reber, Assistant Director for Intelligence Coordination, to the Deputy Director (Intelligence) assesses “flying saucers” as a potential national security concern. It notes that the U.S. Air Force had investigated approximately 1,500 reported sightings through the Air Technical Intelligence Center and had explained all but approximately 20 percent of them. The memorandum states that the Office of Scientific Intelligence had not concluded that the reported objects were created or controlled by the Soviet Union. It identifies priority intelligence questions concerning Soviet knowledge of the phenomena, potential Soviet ability to exploit them against U.S. security interests, and possible effects on the U.S. warning system. It also concludes that the Department of Defense held primary responsibility for initiating fundamental scientific research to develop a comprehensive understanding of the phenomena and improve rapid identification. The memorandum recommends that the Director of Central Intelligence communicate with Secretary of Defense Robert A. Lovett to formalize areas of responsibility as they pertain to unidentified flying objects. It further concludes that available information did not yet provide a basis for psychological-warfare planners to consider employing the phenomena and that a National Intelligence Estimate should precede any development of a public policy intended to reduce or restrain public concern.

Memorandum dated 13 October 1952 to the Deputy Director (Intelligence) concerning flying saucers (unidentified flying objects). The Air Force has observed and analyzed sightings because of the possibility they could be attacks on the U.S. or used by an enemy to exploit resulting confusion. Defense Department research (A-2 through ATIC) has accounted for about 80% of roughly 1,500 reported sightings; about 20% remain unexplained. CIA/OSI judged existing information does not support the conclusion that the saucers are Soviet-created or controlled, but advised that intelligence collection and analysis of Soviet capabilities to produce, launch, or control such objects will not be effective until fundamental scientific research clarifies their nature, causes, and identification methods. Key scientific intelligence questions listed are: (a) Soviet knowledge of the phenomena, (b) possible Soviet capabilities to exploit them against U.S. security, and (c) effects on warning systems. Conclusions: initiating fundamental scientific research is primarily the Defense Department's responsibility; certain papers should be dispatched to Secretary Lovett; it is too early to plan psychological warfare uses of flying saucers; a National Estimate from intelligence would provide a basis for reducing mass hysteria and for public policy. Signed by Q. Reber (Intelligence Coordination). An official CIA routing slip is appended.

AAWSAP’s official scope of work identified 12 technical research areas relating to potential aerospace threats over a time horizon of more than 40 years. As an administrative record, the file documents how AAWSAP was scoped, organized, tasked, funded, or described at a particular point in time. This statement of work establishes the program’s formal mission for exploring far-term foreign aerospace threats by examining possible breakthrough technologies out to 2050 rather than extrapolating from then-current aerospace trends. The document lays out AAWSAP’s research areas and contractual deliverables at program start, including 12 technical topics to be studied, recurring status and management reporting, comprehensive technical reports and briefings for each area, and a final integrated threat assessment. AAWSAP’s official scope of work identified 12 technical research areas relating to potential aerospace threats over a time horizon of more than 40 years. This June 2009 letter from Senator Harry Reid (D-NV) to Deputy Secretary of Defense William Lynn III requests that portions of the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program (AATIP) be placed under a restricted Special Access Program (SAP) with a tightly controlled access list. The letter states that the Senate had directed DIA to assess far-term foreign advanced aerospace threats, describes ongoing technical work aligning with AAWSAP’s program areas, and asserts that the program had already produced several highly sensitive unconventional findings. The attached material proposes a preliminary SAP structure, including a bigoted-access list, a tentative program timeline through Fiscal Year 2013, and continued roles for both government and BAASS personnel. This document is an administrative or programmatic record related to the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP), a Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA)-administered program active from 2008 to 2012. AAWSAP’s official scope of work identified 12 technical research areas relating to potential aerospace threats over a time horizon of more than 40 years. As an administrative record, the file documents how AAWSAP was scoped, organized, tasked, funded, or described at a particular point in time. This November 2009 DIA information memorandum evaluates Senator Harry Reid’s June 2009 request (DOW-UAP-D183) to place portions of the AAWSAP contract, described in his letter under the alternate name “Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program” (AAITP), into a restricted Special Access Program (SAP). The memorandum concludes that DIA could not find adequate justification for such a step, stating that all first-year program documents had been unclassified, that the contractor had not established a secure facility during that period, and that DIA was unaware of any delivered report containing information sensitive enough to warrant additional compartmentation. It further argues that the available material did not meet the threshold for original classification, in part because much of it consisted of publicly available scientific or technical information, and it characterizes Reid’s claims of highly sensitive findings as more plausibly referring to future phases of the effort than to the reports already delivered. In effect, the document is a formal internal finding that Senator Reid’s SAP request was not warranted, grounded in DIA’s view that the program’s first-year outputs did not justify heightened protection beyond normal classification procedures.

DIA（Defense Intelligence Agency）情報メモ。ハリー・リード上院議員からの要請に基づき、Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Application Program Contract（議員の書簡ではAAITPと表記）についての制限付き特別アクセスプログラム（SAP）設置要請をDIA防衛警戒室（DWO）が評価した結果、制限付きSAPを設置する十分な根拠は見当たらないと結論付けている。FY2009に提出されたすべての成果物は非分類（契約業者に安全施設がなく職員がクリアランス審査中のため）であり、FY2010も大部分は非分類の見込みだが、当初の技術報告書のうち4〜6件は外国研究を扱う部分が拡張され派生的に秘（Secret）に分類される可能性がある。プログラム全体を派生的に分類することはDoD 5200.1‑Rの指針から非実用的であり、原始的分類も報告書内容が米国政府の所有・作成・管理下にあるものではなく、基礎科学研究の成果は国家安全保障に明確に関連しない限り分類できないため勧められないと示している。リード議員が指摘する「高度に機微な非伝統的航空宇宙関連発見」については、現時点でDIAはACCMや制限付きSAPに値するほど機微で脆弱な情報を含む報告書を把握しておらず、これらは将来フェーズを指す可能性があると述べ、報告書の草稿はDWOに転送されているため内容確認は同オフィスを通じて行うよう案内している。
DIA information memo. In response to Senator Harry Reid’s request to establish a restricted Special Access Program (SAP) for the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Application Program Contract (referred to in Reid’s letter as AAITP), the DIA Defense Warning Office (DWO) reviewed program deliverables and concluded there is insufficient justification to establish a restricted SAP. All documents delivered in FY2009 were unclassified (contractor lacked a secure facility and staff were pending clearances); most FY2010 products are expected to remain unclassified, though 4–6 original technical reports will be expanded to include classified material and are likely to be derivatively classified at the Secret level due to foreign research content. Classifying the overall program derivatively is impractical under DoD 5200.1‑R guidance, and original classification is inadvisable because the information is not owned/produced/controlled by the U.S. government and basic scientific research/results cannot be classified absent a clear national security nexus. Although Senator Reid cited “several highly sensitive, unconventional aerospace-related findings” requiring extraordinary protection, DIA is not aware of any current reports that warrant ACCM or a restricted SAP and assumes those remarks refer to future phases; draft technical reports from year one have been forwarded to DWO for review and questions should be directed to that office.

The info memo (U-10-2552/CE) from Ronald L. Burgess Jr., Director of the DIA, summarizes the origins, deliverables, and DIA assessment of the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program (AATIP). AATIP was initiated in the FY2008 Defense Supplemental with a $10 million congressional add by Senators Reid and Inouye to study foreign advanced aerospace weapon threats over the next ~40 years and to develop infrastructure for a center of expertise, with emphasis on unconventional or “leap” aerospace vehicles. DIA issued an RFP covering 12 technical areas and awarded the contract to the sole bidder, Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies LLC (BAASS). BAASS, working with academics and scientists, produced 26 technical reports by June 2009 (delivered to DIA by Sept 2009); one report was published in March 2010. The FY2010 appropriations included an additional $12 million, and 12 more reports were produced and delivered. Senator Reid requested establishment of an ACCM or SAP in June 2009; in November 2009 DIA reviewed the program and found insufficient grounds, based on classification levels of current and projected deliverables, to classify the program or invoke ACCM/SAP. This info memo documents the Defense Warning Office (DWO) review of the first-year deliverables (26 technical reports) submitted by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) under the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications contract. The reports cover a broad range of advanced-aerospace topics (e.g., antigravity, metamaterials, invisibility cloaking, positron propulsion, metallic glasses, BioMEMS, superconductors in gravity research, high-energy laser weapons, warp drives, quantum entanglement communications). Reviews—conducted by independent reviewers and including assessments from Sandia National Laboratories—were uniformly positive, with several highly favorable evaluations. DWO plans to publish the reports as Defense Intelligence Studies and distribute them to relevant Defense Department agencies and labs. Draft budget guidance indicates Congress may fund the option year at about $12 million; in FY2010 BAASS will use the FY2009 reports to assess adversary exploitation potential, select studies for classified experimental verification, and perform new classified and unclassified studies with partners, with deliverables due in late summer 2010.

This document is an Air Intelligence Information Report (AIIR), a standardized U.S. Air Force reporting form used to record raw information of potential intelligence value for later analysis. The form served as a primary vehicle for U.S. Air Force field intelligence collection throughout the early Cold War, until defense-wide reporting standards were established in the early 1960s. This AIIR records an October 13, 1957, incident approximately one half-mile south of Great Falls, Viginia, near the Potomac River. At approximately 2105Z (5:05 p.m. local time), two civilians reported observing an unidentified flying object (UFO) while attempting to locate Sputnik, a Soviet satellite. The report describes the object as a single, black, round “dot” with an approximate apparent size comparable to the head of a pin. The report characterizes the object as moving along a true course of 007 degrees directly overhead, as measured with a compass. It also indicates that the object remained in view for approximately 5-6 seconds before being obscured by trees. All descriptive and estimative language contained in this report reflects the reporter’s subjective interpretation at the time of the event. Such characterizations should not be interpreted as a conclusive indication of the presence or absence of any intrinsic object features or performance characteristics.

This AIIR records six observer accounts of incidents reportedly involving unidentified phenomena on November 2 and 3, 1957, in and around the municipalities of Levelland, Smyer, Shallowater, and Sundown, Texas. The report contains descriptions of bright, oval-shaped lights and objects; as well as temporary disruptions to vehicle engines, headlights, radios, and electrical systems. The file summarizes observer interviews and includes sketched depictions of reported objects. It also includes supplementary investigative materials such as a map of the area, weather data, and deconfliction with known aircraft traffic, weather-balloon activity, oil-field gas flaring, and downed power lines. The file also includes comments by the preparing officer, assessing the credibility of the individuals’ reports. He noted inconsistencies among the reports and noted that meteorological explanations may account for a portion of the reported activity. Ultimately, the officer stated that available knowledge within his office and the available evidence were insufficient to resolve the incident. This AIIR documents a November 13, 1957, incident involving two sightings of bright lights in the sky, reported by separate U.S. Army military police patrols near Stallion Site Camp, approximately 90 miles north of White Sands Proving Grounds headquarters. An Air Intelligence report (AISS‑UFOB‑389‑57) documents two separate MP motor‑patrol sightings of unidentified aerial lights near Stallion Site, about 90 miles north of White Sands Proving Grounds in early November 1957. Reported by Det‑5 personnel: (1) Cpl Glenn H. Toy and PFC James E. Wilbanks observed at ~0300Z a very bright, egg‑shaped light that descended to about 50 yards altitude, remained briefly, then went to the ground and extinguished; estimated size varied (roughly 75–100 yards by one account; ~120 ft in another). (2) SP‑3 Henry R. Barlow and SP‑3 Forest R. Oakes at ~0030Z reported a bright, pulsating light that rose to about 45° from the horizon, changed color from reddish to white, appeared fuzzy, and was observed for ~25 minutes before disappearing. Follow‑up inquiries (Univ. of New Mexico meteorology) found no abnormal atmospheric or astronomical phenomena; records show Venus was visible that evening (2000 MST, azimuth 225°, altitude ~15°) and moonset was 0229 MST on 3 Nov. The preparing officer concluded the first sighting was misidentification of the moonset and the second was Venus. Sources were judged young and impressionable and their accounts possibly exaggerated. Investigator: Capt. Patrick O. Shere; preparing officer: Lt. Col. William P. Brunson.

This AIIR documents an October 19, 1957, observation made from the Larson Air Force Base Operations and Control Tower, Washington, from 0110Z to 0250Z (5:10 p.m. to 6:50 p.m. local). The report describes a bright, silvery, apparently circular object observed south-southwest of Moses Lake and moving westward. This sequence suggests that the term functioned as an operational assessment or identifier indicating that the reported object did not warrant interception. On 20 Oct 1957 between 01:10Z and 02:50Z a UFO was sighted SSW of Moses Lake, Washington, observed from Larson AFB operations roof and control tower with naked eye and field glasses. The object appeared circular/ball-shaped, silver and intermittently changed color (light blue, golden, pink, pinkish-red), was sometimes very bright, and showed a brief apparent splitting and reforming; no tail/exhaust or sound was noted. Extract from a USAF report (OAirA, Lima IR-364-57; report date 29 Nov 1957). A qualified weather observer at the Compania Peruana de Servicios Meteorologicos S.A., located on the continental divide about 35 miles S of Cajamarca (elevation 3,750 m; 07°25′30″S, 78°20′30″W), observed and recorded an unidentified flying object using an automatic Zeiss recording theodolite. Initial sighting occurred about noon on 26 Oct 1957 (described as white, steel-gleaming, visible for more than 15 minutes); further observations were made on 28 Oct, 29 Oct, 7 Nov and 8 Nov 1957. The report contains detailed GMT-timed azimuth and elevation measurements with visibility notes (tables of times, azimuths, elevations and cloud/visibility conditions), and on 28 Oct the moon’s position was measured for comparison. The theodolite was fixed on a concrete base and not moved; recorder-disk calculations gave motion ranges—one session showed a total change over 124 minutes of +21.2° elevation and +33.8° azimuth, another session over 94 minutes showed +17.2° elevation and +19.2° azimuth. No identification of the object is provided.

An Air Intelligence Information Report (IR-1-57) documents a UFO sighting over Abingdon, Virginia on 6 November 1957 at 1735 EST reported by CHARLES N. BOOTH, HARRY L. COOMS, and MARGARET (C.) MAST. Witnesses consistently reported a single bright red-orange object at high altitude observed for about five minutes, moving on a straight course until disappearing below the horizon, with no sound and no other air traffic observed; weather was clear with good visibility. BOOTH described a carrot-shaped object (appearing about 12–14 ft long in his perception, narrow end up), COOMS described an elongated-egg shape with a short rocket-like exhaust section (about one-third of the object's length) but no trailing contrail, and MAST gave a similar high-altitude red-orange-light description. The sighting was relayed through CIC and 21st District OSI to Major Clarke E. Johnston, 345th Bomb Wing, who reported lacking means to collect further data and requested 21st District OSI to assemble required information per AFR 200-2. This document is an Air Intelligence Information Report (AIIR), a standardized U.S. Air Force reporting form used to record raw information of potential intelligence value for later analysis. The form served as a primary vehicle for U.S. Air Force field intelligence collection throughout the early Cold War, until defense-wide reporting standards were established in the early 1960s. This AIIR records a December 17, 1956, incident in the vicinity of Ube, Japan, in which two U.S. Air Force F-86D pilots were conducting practice intercepts under ground-controlled radar direction when one pilot reported detecting a second radar target, separate from the other F-86D, at a range of 20 nautical miles. The report states that the unidentified return appeared larger than the return from the other aircraft and remained visible on the interceptor’s radar scope for approximately seven to eight minutes. It further states that the pilot later obtained intermittent visual contact for approximately three to four minutes after closing to within about five nautical miles, describing the object as best resembling the upper half of a sphere. The report also notes possible electronic countermeasures interference on the F-86D radar scope and estimates the object’s rate of departure at 1,500 to 1,800 knots (1,726–2,071 mph) after the radar return moved rapidly off the top of the scope, while noting that the figure exceeded what the radar set could directly indicate for a negative rate of closure. The report further states that neither ground-based radar sites nor the second pilot acquired the object on radar. All descriptive and estimative language contained in this report reflects the reporter’s subjective interpretation at the time of the event. Such characterizations should not be interpreted as a conclusive indication of the presence or absence of any intrinsic object features or performance characteristics.

Report IR-12-57. On 17 December 1956 two F-86D pilots of the 66th Fighter-Interceptor Squadron (1st Lt R. Brumet and R.A. Sneary), operating under GCI near Ube, Japan (approx. 33°39'N, 131°18'E), detected a second radar target about 20 nm away. The unknown return remained on Brumet's radar for about 7–8 minutes and was visually seen intermittently for 3–4 minutes. Brumet visually described an object roughly the size/shape of a pencil eraser on the windshield, upper-half appearing spherical, bottom circular, color gold-tan. He closed to about 4–5 nm but could not get closer. Brumet's radar briefly showed a closure rate of 600–700 kt; after a slight turn the radar track moved rapidly off the top of the scope and disappeared, with an estimated departure speed of 1500–1800 kt. During the incident Brumet experienced interference pulses on the GIZZLE band (similar to ECM); an anti-jam frequency change removed the interference for several seconds. Sneary's AI radar did not detect the object but showed a cluster of small bright pinpoints at 12 nm. No ground radar sites reported the track; aircraft and systems were inspected and found satisfactory. Pilot flight-time and witness statements are recorded in the file.

This file contains a confirmed, complete, high-quality digitization of reports by Lockheed Aircraft Corporation personnel concerning the observation of an unidentified flying object (UFO) near Agoura and Point Mugu, California, on December 16, 1953. Clarence L. Johnson, Lockheed’s Chief Engineer, transmitted the reports to the Air Technical Intelligence Center at Wright Patterson Air Force Base for scientific evaluation, along with a request for comments regarding the incident. The file also includes individual accounts from Johnson and Lockheed flight-test personnel. This report is significant, due to Johnson’s reputation as one of the foremost aerospace engineers in American history, and his virtually unmatched familiarity with high-performance aircraft. Johnson reported observing a dark, elliptical object from his ranch west of Agoura at approximately 5:00 p.m. He initially considered whether it might be a cloud or smoke trail; he reported that it appeared stationary for several minutes before moving westward and disappearing. Separately, personnel aboard a Lockheed test flight reported seeing an object in the vicinity of Point Mugu while flying off the southern California coast at approximately the same time. Their accounts described an apparently stationary, dark, wing-like or elongated object that moved westward and disappeared from view.

概要: 1953年12月16日夕方（現地時間約17:00、報告では5:00–5:05）にカリフォルニア州アゴーラ周辺および海上（Point Mugu / Santa Barbara Islands方面）で、ロッキード社の複数の職員が同一の未確認飛行物体を目撃した。主要な目撃者はClarence L. Johnson（主任技術者、地上）、R. L. Thoren（主任飛行試験技師）、R. E. Wimmer（試験機パイロット）、J. F. Ware（飛行試験技術者）、P. A. Colman（主任空力技術者）などである。観察の共通点は以下の通り: 物体は最初黒い静止した雲状（レンズ状）に見え、楕円形で長短比およそ7–10:1、紅い夕景を背景に輪郭が明瞭であった。地上・機上双方で数分（報告上は合計約5–7分）観察され、当初はほとんど動かず、その後急に西方へ高速で長い浅い上昇軌跡を取り、1–2分ないし90秒程度で視認から消失した。高度は機上観測で約16,000–20,000フィート、物体の距離・大きさは不確定。目撃は複数の訓練を受けた観察者によって時刻・位置が一致して報告されている。報告書は1954年1月にロッキードから空軍の調査機関へ提出され、報道には公開されていない。報告には物的証拠の提示はなく（写真等の添付は示されていない）。
Summary: On 16 December 1953 at about local 17:00 (reports cite ~5:00–5:05 PM), multiple Lockheed personnel independently observed the same unidentified aerial object near Agoura, California and offshore toward Point Mugu / the Santa Barbara Islands. Principal witnesses included Clarence L. Johnson (Chief Engineer, ground observer), R. L. Thoren (Chief Flight Test Engineer), R. E. Wimmer (Engineering Test Pilot), J. F. Ware (flight test engineer), and P. A. Colman (Chief Aerodynamics Engineer). Common observational details: the object first appeared as a dark, stationary lenticular/cloud-like silhouette, elliptical in shape with an approximate major/minor axis ratio of 7–10:1, sharply outlined against the red sunset. It was observed from both the ground and a WV-2 aircraft for several minutes (reports cite roughly 5–7 minutes), remained essentially stationary initially, then suddenly moved rapidly westward in a long shallow climb and disappeared within about 1–2 minutes (90 seconds noted in one account). Aircraft observers were at roughly 16,000–20,000 ft; distance and dimensions of the object were not determined. Multiple trained observers reported consistent times and locations. Lockheed forwarded the reports to the Air Force investigative group in January 1954; the material was not released to the press and no physical evidence (e.g., confirmed photographs) is provided in the submitted reports.

This file contains documentation of three visual observations of aerial lights near Fontana and La Jolla, California, on August 22, 1956. The first two reports, from the Fontana area, described a single bright red light with a fiery tail resembling a comet or an aircraft using afterburner. The reporting individuals described the light as moving slowly westward toward Catalina Island, with an estimated speed of 115 knots (132 mph). A third report from La Jolla described two yellow-white lights moving slowly, making turns while maintaining formation, and fading into light fog or haze. The summary card preceding the observer accounts records the Air Force evaluation of all three reports as being attributable to aircraft.

This file contains a U.S. Air Force Project 10073 Record Card and associated material documenting six visual reports of unidentified flying objects from locations across Southern California. The reports occurred between 0306Z and 0310Z on 1 December 1957 (7:06 p.m. to 7:10 p.m. Pacific Standard Time on 30 November local time) and included locations near San Clemente Island, Borrego Springs, Blythe, Oxnard, Ventura, and San Bernardino. Civilian and military observers described a bright object moving generally northeastward. Accounts variously characterized the object as a falling star, bright light, or ball, with some reporting a bluish-white or reddish color, flame, or a trailing tail. Individual observation durations ranged from several seconds to approximately 30 seconds. The record card states that the Air Force evaluated the object to be astronomical in nature, attributing the incident to a meteor. Associated messages state that Air Defense Command personnel and Mount Wilson Observatory also assessed reported objects as meteors.

一部公開済み
documents.summaryText:
複数ページの報告は南カリフォルニア域での同時刻帯の地上目視目撃をまとめたもので、報告時刻として文書中に01/0306Z、01/0308Z、01/0309Z、01/0310Zなどが記載される。目撃記述はいずれも単一の球状（野球大）物体で、青白い強光に包まれ白青色の炎または尾を引き、炎が後方へ吹き形成された“円錐形”やピン程度の細い尾があるとされた。持続時間は概ね5〜30秒で、移動は南東から北、あるいは南西から北北東などの方位を報告するものがある。高度に関する記載は、操縦士の24,000ft報告や観測者の推定で50,000〜75,000ftから地上へ向かう旨などが含まれる。観測者は海軍・空軍の軍人や民間人（氏名の記載あり）で、ADCCやマウントウィルソン天文台は大きな流星（meteor）であると判断した記録が複数ある。オックスナード等から戦闘機が緊急発進したが捜索は否定的結果であった旨も含まれている。文書は複数の送受信コードを伴う公電形式の集約で、最終結論として報告群の多くが流星と見なしていることが明記されている。
The documents compile multiple ground-visual reports from Southern California at roughly the same times (noted entries include 01/0306Z, 01/0308Z, 01/0309Z, 01/0310Z, among others). Witnesses consistently described a single, round ("baseball-sized") object emitting bright blue-white light, enveloped in white/blue flame, with a cone-shaped flame flow and a very small (pin-sized) tail. Durations reported were about 5–30 seconds, and trajectories were reported generally from south/southwest toward north/northeast or similar headings. Altitude references include a pilot report at 24,000 ft and some observer estimates suggesting descent from 50,000–75,000 ft toward the ground. Observers included military personnel and civilians (named in reports); ADCC and the Mt. Wilson Observatory are recorded as concluding the object was a large meteor. Fighter sorties were launched from nearby bases for search but yielded negative results. The file is a collection of tactical messages and record cards; the predominant assessment in the record is that the sightings were meteors.

Locations listed include Fontana, California and "8 miles east of Montana, Calif." The witnesses are listed as "MR/MRS WALTER HAMILTON" (11738 Miller St, Montana, Calif). This file contains a U.S. Air Force Project 10073 Record Card and related correspondence, including drawn depictions, concerning a reported observation of an unidentified flying object from San Pedro, California, on November 30, 1966. Two observers described seeing a bright light in the direction of Catalina Island. The record card summarizes the reported object as white with a red center, brighter than the brightest star, and comparable in brightness to the moon. It records that the object moved northwest and disappeared slowly after an observation lasting approximately five minutes and 10 seconds. The file also includes a March 15, 1967, Air Force letter requesting that one of the reporting individuals complete a technical questionnaire because the information initially received was insufficient for a scientific evaluation. In the completed questionnaire, the observer described seeing the object outdoors from San Pedro at approximately 5:45 p.m. Pacific Standard Time and stated that an airplane appeared to approach before the object began to disappear. The Air Force assessed the reported object as a possible hot-air balloon. However, the file does not document the basis for that assessment.

This file contains U.S. Air Force investigative records and related correspondence concerning two separate reported observations of unidentified flying objects in Southern California on June 17, 1949. The materials include an Office of Special Investigations report regarding an observation from La Jolla and a later Air Materiel Command inquiry into a report from Glendale. In the La Jolla report, an observer described seeing one large, bright, round object at approximately 11:10 a.m. local time. The individual estimated that the object was about four miles away and 4,000 feet above the ground, compared its apparent size to a Douglas DC-4 aircraft, and described it as resembling a “chromium plated pie tin.” The report states that the object moved rapidly away, made a wide turn, and remained visible for approximately 30 seconds. A separate report documents an observation from a moving automobile near Grand Central Airport in Glendale at approximately 3:30 p.m. local time. The reporting individual described two bright metallic, oval objects that reflected sunlight, approached from the northeast, traveled slowly across the valley, then tilted and departed rapidly toward the northwest. The objects remained in view for approximately one and a half minutes. The Project 10073 Record Card associated with the Glendale observation assessed the reported objects as aircraft, stating that the available information did not indicate that they could not have been aircraft. The file does not document a comparable final evaluation of the La Jolla report.
